source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5893695 (full text read in own browser tab: abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusions, footnotes) and the correction, PMC HTML PMC6713697 (doi 10.1007/s00213-018-4886-8, reached from the article's own correction link). The correction changes only the licence (CC BY 4.0 from 19 March 2018, retrospective open access) and the spelling of a co-author's name (Timmermann); no data or conclusions changed. Figures 1-4 not read as images (captions read); supplementary tables of themes and quotations and the playlist not read.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim is markedly more cautious than the source, whose title, abstract and conclusions say music plays a central (mediating) therapeutic role and that outcomes suffered when music was disliked, on the basis of uncontrolled correlations in 19 patients. 'The raters agreed only moderately (r 0.6)' is the editors' reading; the authors call average r = 0.6 'good'.
claims.note: Every Kaelen number checked. Editors' intervals recomputed (Fisher z, n = 19): r = 0.60 -> 0.200 to 0.828; 0.59 -> 0.185 to 0.824; 0.57 -> 0.156 to 0.814; 0.004 -> -0.451 to 0.457: all match. Counts 18/19, 17, 15, 10, 10/19, 9/19, 6/19 (dissonance 4 of 6) match. Two qualifications: (1) 'one standard playlist' had one exception: patient #6, who strongly disliked the music in the first session, heard a Johns Hopkins playlist in the second; (2) the printed p for openness and QIDS (p = .001) cannot be right for r = 0.57 with n = 19 (recomputed p = 0.011), which still passes the stated FDR threshold of 0.016. The interview and the QIDS outcome were both taken 1 week after the 25 mg session; the paper does not literally say 'the same visit', but both are at that time point.

anchors.locator: Methods > Participants (1st paragraph); Methods > Experiment overview and procedures (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: 19 patients with treatment-resistant major depression (HAM-D 21-item score 17 or more; no improvement after at least two antidepressants for at least 6 weeks in the current episode); part of the larger uncontrolled safety and efficacy study of psilocybin (Carhart-Harris et al. 2016a). QIDS-SR16 (patient-rated) at screening (baseline) and post-treatment.

anchors.locator: Methods > Experiment overview and procedures (2nd to 4th paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Preparation visit of about 4 h including listening to session music with eye-shades; two psilocybin sessions one week apart (10 mg, then 25 mg; study conditions); one patient and two therapists per session; QIDS at baseline and 1 week after the second session; 11D-ASC at the end of a session; drug intensity self-rated on a 0-100 VAS after each session; music interview always 1 week after the 25 mg session.

anchors.locator: Methods > Therapeutic setting (1st paragraph); Methods > Music selection (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Specially designed therapy room in the Clinical Research Facility at Imperial College London (medical equipment hidden, adjusted lighting, cushions, plants, art); patients lay on a bed with eye-shades; two therapists checked in every 30-60 min; standardised playlist started at ingestion, via headphones or speaker. Exception: patient #6 strongly disliked the first-session music and heard a Johns Hopkins playlist in the second session.

anchors.locator: Methods > The semi-structured interview (1st paragraph); Results (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Interview 1 week after the final session, by the same researcher except once, covering both sessions; four open questions including positive and negative influences of the music. Welcome influences in 18 of 19 patients (95%); unwelcome influences in 10 of 19 (53%); appreciated styles in 19 of 19; unappreciated styles in 11 of 19.

anchors.locator: Results > Welcome influences: intensification (1st paragraph); Welcome influences of the music: guidance (1st paragraph); Welcome influence of the music: calming (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Intensification of the experience 17 of 19 (89%); guidance 15 of 19 (79%); calming 10 of 19 (53%).

anchors.locator: Results > Unwelcome influences of the music: intensification (1st paragraph); resistance to music-evoked experience (1st paragraph); misguidance (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Among the 10 with unwelcome influences: music intensified unwanted emotions (fearfulness, sadness) in 5, created discomfort in 5, irritation in 4. Resistance to the music-evoked experience 9 of 19 (47%). Misguidance 6 of 19 (32%), mostly music felt as a mismatch with the unfolding experience ('dissonance', 4 of 6).

anchors.locator: Methods > Ratings for music experience (1st and 2nd paragraphs); Methods > Correlation analyses (2nd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Liking, resonance and openness were chosen from the coding as hypothesised predictors; four researchers blind to patient identifiers and treatment outcomes rated each patient from the interview transcript on 0-100 VAS; ratings averaged. Outcome: percentage reduction in QIDS from baseline to 1 week after the 25 mg session; Pearson correlations, FDR control.

anchors.locator: Results > Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes (2nd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: QIDS reduction with liking r = 0.60 (p = .006), resonance r = 0.59 (p = .008), openness r = 0.57 (printed p = .001; recomputed about 0.011); with drug intensity r = 0.004 (p = 0.98). FDR-adjusted significance threshold 0.016. Editors' 95% intervals (Fisher z, n = 19): 0.20 to 0.83, 0.19 to 0.82, 0.16 to 0.81, -0.45 to 0.46.

anchors.locator: Results > Inter-rating reliability and discriminative validity of music experience variables (1st paragraph); Discussion > Music experience predicts experience and therapy outcomes (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Inter-rater agreement average r = 0.6 (+/- 0.1) over 18 correlations, called good by the authors; the three music variables intercorrelated r = 0.9, 0.96 and 0.91, which the authors say likely represent one construct; drug intensity correlated with none of them.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Limitations and future directions (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: No placebo condition, so causal inferences are problematic; data mainly qualitative, so the magnitude of themes could not be studied; the study is presented as a patient perspective generating hypotheses.

anchors.locator: Abstract > Results and Conclusions; Discussion > Implications for the use of music in psychedelic therapy (1st paragraph); Conclusions
anchors.extracted: Authors write that music experience was significantly predictive of depression reductions, that outcomes suffered when music was dissonant, disliked or resisted, and that music plays a central (mediating) therapeutic role: causal wording from unadjusted correlations in 19 uncontrolled patients, with the music rated after the outcome had occurred.

key_findings.note: QIDS at screening is stated in Experiment overview and procedures, 1st paragraph, and 'covering both sessions' in The semi-structured interview (1st paragraph); the locator could add both.
Intervals and the p discrepancy found independently in step 1 (recomputed p = 0.0108).
The paper prints 'average r = 0.6 +/- 0.1' without saying whether 0.1 is an SD; 'SD' is the card's reading.
Full locator: Discussion > Limitations and future directions, 1st paragraph.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: r = 0.53 gives p = 0.0196, r = 0.535 gives about 0.018.
The Results speak of mystical experience 'during the psilocybin sessions' (plural) without saying which session's ASC and VAS entered the correlations.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high: two high domains (confounding by overall session quality; an exposure rated from interviews at the outcome visit) that could each produce the association, which fits ROBINS-E's rule for very high when several high domains substantially lower confidence.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial (arguably severe): 'central mediating role' and 'outcomes suffered' rest on uncontrolled, unadjusted correlations in 19 patients with no mediation test; the limitations paragraph concedes the causal problem.

missed: Minor: self-rated drug intensity correlated with none of the three music ratings (Results > Inter-rating reliability and discriminative validity of music experience variables, 1st paragraph), the authors' basis for treating music experience as distinct from drug intensity; not among the key findings.
